title: ÆTHER: First Love v12 (love + energy + Indian touch)
story: A boy sees a girl for the first time and feels he can fly: the glance, shyness, attraction, togetherness, the dream, the celebration of love.

brief.notes: Jithesh 30 Oct 07:42 on v11: 'got the right mood, right language, but it doesn't have that Indian touch.' v12 = v11 unchanged in mood, key, energy and six parts, with the Indian touch in the WRITING (music-scoring 9 rule 15, music.md 17): raga melody phrased like a South Indian playback singer (gamakam, grace-note turns, repeated-note runs, bent held notes), flute-violin question and answer, Indian-style violin unison, modal harmony over a pedal bass, film-song interludes, tabla/dholak keherwa bounce leading the groove. Prompt mode (music_v2).

prompt: A brand-new romantic and uplifting love anthem written the way today's great Tamil and Telugu film composers write a hit love theme for the hero meeting the girl for the first time: LOVE plus ENERGY. It is romantic, happy, hopeful and inspiring, with a rising, heart-lifting energy, like falling in love and feeling you can fly. Not sad, not sleepy, not calm background music, not a dance number. Instrumental. Key: a bright, warm major key all the way through. INDIAN TOUCH, in the writing style of a Tamil or Telugu film love song (the style, not just the instruments): the melody is built on a raga like Kalyani or Mohanam and phrased the way a South Indian playback singer sings, with gamakam slides into notes, quick grace-note turns and short repeated-note runs, then a long held note that bends at the end of each phrase; question-and-answer phrases between flute and violin; the hook comes back bigger each time. The violin section plays the tune in Indian-style unison with slides, not just Western chord pads; the harmony stays modal over a pedal bass, with a bass line that moves with the melody. The interludes are film-song style: fast, ornamented flute and violin-section runs in unison, a short tabla flourish, then the tune lands back. Sound: warm and full, with a deep round bass and lush strings, not thin or sparkly. Every real instrument is close and natural, played by real musicians: a soft bansuri flute, a warm solo violin, a felt piano and a clean acoustic guitar, with no heavy echo on them. A soft wordless female voice joins the biggest moments. Rhythm: the classic South Indian film love-song groove at about 92 BPM from 6 s to the end, never stopping: a tabla and dholak keherwa pattern with its swinging Indian bounce leads the groove, supported by a deep warm kick and a soft clap; finger snaps and a light shaker; piano and acoustic guitar answer the melody instead of strumming Western chords all the time. Energetic and forward-moving, but not a dance number. Six parts, each bigger than the last, a new color every 6-8 seconds: 0-6 s THE GLANCE: piano and flute play the rising love call; a soft swell. 6-16 s SHYNESS: the groove starts with kick and tabla; flute and violin trade short smiling phrases. 16-30 s ATTRACTION: the full love melody on the flute, strings and bass driving underneath. 30-44 s TOGETHERNESS: violin and flute play the melody together in harmony, the drums fuller, guitar strumming. 44-54 s THE DREAM: an inspiring build, strings climb, drums build with a fill, the energy rises. 54-70 s THE CELEBRATION OF LOVE: the biggest, happiest, most inspiring moment: the full melody soaring on strings, flute and the female voice together, full drums and bass, goosebumps. 70-76 s: the love call once more, landing on a warm, bright final chord. Not a Western pop ballad, not Hollywood, not generic stock music. Not sad, not dark, not slow, not ambient, not a lullaby, no heavy echo, no EDM, no white-noise risers, no side-chain pumping, no pauses.
